title: Meeting Rooms II
description: Find the minimum number of rooms needed for overlapping meetings using a min-heap of end times.

data.text: Given an array of meeting time intervals `[start, end]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no two meetings overlap in the same room. A meeting ending at time `t` frees the room for a meeting starting at `t`.

**Input:** `intervals = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]`

**Output:** `2`

**Explanation:** `[0,30]` overlaps both others, which do not overlap each other, so two rooms suffice.
Count, for each meeting, how many others overlap it, and take the maximum. Such a pairwise comparison cannot count overlaps correctly without a sweep, and costs O(n²).

data.title: Peak-overlap brute force O(n²)
data.content: For each interval, count how many intervals contain its start.

data.text: Approach 2: Sort by Start, Min-Heap of End Times

Sort meetings by start time. Keep a min-heap of the end times of meetings currently in progress. For each new meeting, if the earliest-ending meeting has already finished, that room is reusable — pop it. Then push the new end time. The heap size after each step is the number of rooms in use, and its maximum is the answer.

data.title: Min-heap of end times — O(n log n)
data.content: The heap tracks when each occupied room becomes free.

data.title: Only one room needs checking
data.text: You only ever need to ask about the meeting that ends soonest, because if any room is free, that one is. That is exactly what a min-heap gives you in O(log n).

data.title: `<=` allows back-to-back meetings
data.text: Use `<=` rather than `<`: a meeting starting exactly when another ends does not need a new room. Whether this is correct depends on the problem statement, so read it carefully — it is a favourite place to hide an edge case.

Sort all start times and all end times separately, then sweep with two pointers. Count active meetings by incrementing on a start and decrementing on an end, tracking the peak. This is O(n log n) with no heap at all.

data.title: Sort-both sweep — O(n log n), no heap
data.content: The heap's work is replaced by sorting the end times.

data.caption: Sorted by start time, the heap holds the end time of every ongoing meeting; expired end times are popped before the new one is added.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A["[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]"] --> B["add [0,30]: heap [30], rooms 1"]
    B --> C["start 5, heap min 30 > 5: add [5,10] heap [10,30], rooms 2"]
    C --> D["start 15, heap min 10 <= 15: pop 10"]
    D --> E["add [15,20] heap [20,30], rooms 2"]
    E --> F["answer 2"]
    style F fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: This is the interval variant of 'maximum concurrent events', which is why the heap-of-end-times and the two-array sweep give the same answer. The heap version is preferable when you also need to say *which* room each meeting uses.
